opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the more surprising things about pretraining: what a model learns about coding doesn't only come from code. When people think about coding ability, they imagine GitHub repositories, clean functions, and documentation. That's a big part of it, but the internet is much messier, and the mess turns out to matter.

Take a forum thread where someone posts broken code, gets an error message, tries a fix, and someone else explains why it still doesn't work. That's not polished code. It's a record of the *process* of debugging, a back-and-forth between hypothesis and feedback. A model that reads millions of these absorbs something like the shape of iterative problem-solving, not just the syntax of the final answer. So when we later ask it to act as an agent, run code, read a stack trace, and try again, part of that behavior was already latent in the pretraining distribution.

There are subtler effects too. Mathematical writing, formal logic, even well-structured natural-language explanations seem to transfer to code. The underlying skill of decomposing a problem, keeping track of state, and being precise about what follows from what isn't specific to Python. Conversely, code seems to help reasoning in other domains. So the boundaries between data types are much blurrier than our labels suggest.

The other side is that the data also brings habits you might not want. The internet is full of code that's outdated, insecure, or written to pass a quick test rather than to be correct. It has lots of "it works on my machine" fixes and copy-pasted snippets. The model learns the statistics of what people actually write, not what they should write. So some of the quirks we see, like a model making a test pass in a hacky way or reaching for a deprecated library, reflect the distribution it was raised on as much as anything that happens in post-training.

That's why I think of pretraining as giving the model a very broad prior: a sense of what's possible and what code in the world looks like. Then post-training, especially reinforcement learning with real execution feedback, sharpens it and pushes it toward what actually works. But you can't fully separate the two. A lot of what looks like a capability we "added" later was really unlocked from something already in the data. Understanding which signals in pretraining produce which downstream behaviors is still pretty under-explored. We have intuitions, but not a clean science yet.

r001.rationale: The response says GitHub repositories, clean functions, and documentation are a big part of coding ability, but it does not connect the relatively high quality of code in unfiltered internet data to models’ strong ability to generate code snippets.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's a lot less clean than people imagine. When you hear "pretraining on code," you picture GitHub repos going in and coding ability coming out. But a huge amount of what makes a model good at code isn't the code itself—it's everything surrounding the code on the internet.

Think about where code actually lives online. It's on Stack Overflow, with a question, a wrong answer, a comment saying "this doesn't work on Python 3," and then the fix. It's in GitHub issues where someone pastes a stack trace and three people argue about the root cause. It's in blog posts where someone explains why they refactored something. It's in commit messages, pull request reviews, forum threads from 2009. That data is noisy and messy, but it's incredibly rich, because it captures the process of programming, not just the artifact. The artifact is the final file. The process is debugging, reasoning about what went wrong, changing your mind. And it turns out the process is much of what you want the model to learn.

So there's this somewhat surprising thing where "low quality" data in the conventional sense—arguments, failed attempts, half-finished explanations—can actually teach things that a clean corpus of perfect code can't. A perfectly clean repository tells you what good code looks like. It doesn't tell you how to get there from a broken state. And agentic coding is almost entirely about getting there from a broken state.

The other side of it is that data shapes the model in ways you didn't intend. Models pick up the conventions, the idioms, the biases of whatever's most abundant. If most Python online is a certain style, the model writes that style, even when it isn't appropriate. If a particular library is over-represented, the model reaches for it reflexively. And the time distribution of the data matters too—a model can be weirdly confident about an API that was deprecated years ago, simply because the internet has more text from the era when that API was popular.

And then there's the transfer that goes the other way, which I find even more interesting: non-code data improving code. Math, logic puzzles, carefully written technical explanations—these seem to help with the reasoning part of coding. There's evidence that mixing in natural language reasoning improves code and vice versa. So the boundary between "code data" and "not code data" is much blurrier than people treat it.

What I've come to believe is that you shouldn't think of pretraining as installing skills. It's more like you're shaping a prior. The internet is this enormous, weird, accidental record of how humans think about programming, and the model inherits all of it—the good habits, the bad habits, the arguments, the folklore. Then the job of post-training and RL is to take that prior and push it toward what you actually want. But you can only push so far. The prior matters a lot, and a lot of it was never designed by anyone. It just happened to be what people wrote down.

r001.rationale: The response credits noisy discussions and process data, plus non-code reasoning, with helping coding ability. It does not suggest that relatively high-quality code in unfiltered internet pretraining partly explains models’ strong code-snippet generation.

astra-6.text:
I think the surprising part is that coding ability doesn’t come only from reading code. Internet pretraining mixes code with documentation, tutorials, discussions, bug reports, and people explaining how they solved a problem. A model can learn connections across those things: how an informal request maps to a formal specification, how an error message relates to a mistake, or how to break a task into smaller steps.

Even text that isn’t explicitly about programming might contribute. Following a complicated explanation or keeping track of constraints in a puzzle could help with aspects of coding. But I’d be careful about claiming that any particular kind of data causes a particular capability. These abilities emerge from a mixture, and it’s hard to separate the contributions without controlled experiments.

There’s also a distinction between producing code that looks familiar and solving a new problem. Internet data contains repeated examples, common solutions, and sometimes benchmark problems themselves. So when a model gets better at a coding test, we have to ask: did it learn a reusable abstraction, or did the task become more familiar? Both can improve the score, but they imply very different things about how reliably the model will work on something new.

r001.rationale: The response says internet pretraining includes code and related materials, but it does not suggest that code data is relatively high quality within unfiltered internet data or that this partly explains models’ strong code snippet generation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the surprising part is that coding ability doesn’t come only from code. Internet pretraining mixes code with documentation, tutorials, questions, bug reports, and ordinary language. Those sources can teach a model different parts of the same task: what someone wants, how a problem is described, what a solution might look like, and why a particular approach fails.

For example, a discussion about a bug may contain very little working code, but it can show the connection between an error message and its underlying cause. A tutorial can explain when an algorithm is useful. Those connections matter when the user gives you an ambiguous request rather than a precise programming specification.

But I would be careful about attributing a capability to any particular kind of data just by looking at the model’s behavior. These effects are entangled. You need controlled experiments—changing the data mixture and measuring what improves—to distinguish a plausible story from an actual explanation. The interesting question is not just how much code the model has seen, but what the surrounding data helps it learn to do with that code.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how varied internet sources may contribute to coding ability, but it does not suggest that relatively high-quality code data in unfiltered pretraining explains models’ strong code-snippet generation.
